Purpose: To evaluate the 12-month physicochemical stability of silver and selenium nanoparticles (NPs) fabricated initially for topical caries arrest. Materials and Methods: The nanoparticles were synthesised via chemical reduction and capped with naturally derived agents.
Keywords: silver nanoparticles, selenium nanoparticles, capping agents, shelf-life, colloidal stability, caries arrest, aggregation, agglomeration · The antimicrobial performance, safety, and translational potential of nanoparticles (NPs) in biomedical applications are largely defined by their long-term stability [1]. The antimicrobial activity of metallic and metalloid NPs can change over time owing to changes in their physicochemical properties [2]. Deterioration may manifest as aggregation/agglomeration, oxidation/reduction, dissolution or sedimentation, and is reflected in alterations to particle size, morphology, surface characteristics, surface charge and ion release.
For example, when citrate-capped AgNPs were assessed over 104 days, some particles remained stable, while others aggregated [17]. Another study reported that Lycium barbarum polysaccharide–protein-stabilised SeNPs were stable for 40 days at 4 °C [18]. Therefore, the present study aimed to evaluate the long-term (12-month) physicochemical stability of synthesised silver and selenium NPs under controlled storage conditions, to identify factors that affect their structural integrity and functional performance.
Image analysis and particle size measurements were performed in ImageJ (version 1.53m, NIH, Bethesda, MD, USA) using at least 100 nanoparticles to obtain representative data. TEM imaging was conducted at baseline and at 12 months for the same batch to assess changes in particle morphology during long-term storage. For each NP formulation, one independent synthesis batch (n = 1) was evaluated at baseline and after 12 months of storage.

Nano silver fluoride (NSF), which combines silver nanoparticles with fluoride, was more effective than control in arresting pediatric caries at both 5- and 12-month follow-up in randomized trials (Nagireddy et al., 2019).

A systematic review of antimicrobial restorative materials found consistent evidence of laboratory antimicrobial activity but limited evidence that these effects translate into reduced caries clinically (do Amaral et al., 2016).
Thus, within the evidence considered here, randomized clinical trials evaluating a direct caries-arrest endpoint were available for nano silver fluoride (Nagireddy et al., 2019; Quritum et al., 2024). However, these findings apply to a topical formulation and should not be extrapolated to metallic nanoparticles incorporated into restorative materials.
This distinction is important: the restorative-material studies summarized above primarily demonstrate antimicrobial activity, whereas the NSF trials measured caries arrest and therefore provide direct anticaries evidence (Nagireddy et al., 2019; Quritum et al., 2024). Poor target selection, an uncontrollable manner in drug releasing, poor water solubility, high cost of the PSs, and low oxygen concentrations in deeper parts of the targeted tissues are some factors limiting PS usage in future clinical trials ( Yin et al., 2015 ). context.snippet: ## Abstract Purpose: To evaluate the 12-month physicochemical stability of silver and selenium nanoparticles (NPs) fabricated initially for topical caries arrest. Materials and Methods: The nanoparticles were synthesised via chemical reduction and capped with naturally derived agents. Post-synthesis suspensions were washed and stored at 4 °C in the dark for 12 months. Stability was assessed by comparing the physicochemical properties at baseline and 12 months. The characterisation approaches included Tyndall scattering and UV–visible spectroscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy. Results: As formulations aged, they showed differences in stability. Citrate-capped silver NPs (AgL1) retained a defined surface plasmon resonance and showed a 6.7% reduction in elemental concentration. Silver NPs capped with casein (Ag1) and bovine serum albumin (Ag2) showed moderate reductions in elemental concentration (26.9% and 54.8%, respectively), accompanied by the formation of larger particle populations (~20–40 nm). Their initial mean particle sizes were 3.6 ± 3.4 nm for Ag1 and 2.5 ± 0.8 nm for Ag2. In contrast, silver NPs capped with citrate and tannic acid (AgL2) exhibited a substantial reduction in elemental concentration (88.6%), accompanied by pronounced particle aggregation. Selenium nanoparticles were the least stable: UV–Vis absorption features collapsed, TEM showed agglomeration (>70–100 nm), and ICP–OES indicated a significant reduction in the measured elemental concentration in the analysed suspension especially in Se1 (99.9%) and Se2 (99.96%). context.snippet: Topical cariostatic agents have become a reasonable alternative for managing dental caries in young children. Silver diamine fluoride (SDF) is a practical topical approach to arrest caries and avoid extensive and risky dental treatment. However, the literature demonstrates a parental hesitation towards accepting SDF because of black unaesthetic tooth discolouration following application. The rapid oxidation of ionic silver darkens demineralised tooth structure permanently. In this regard, nano-metallic antimicrobials could augment or substitute for silver, and thereby enhance SDF aesthetic performance. Recently, biomedical research has drawn attention to selenium nanoparticles (SeNPs) due to their antimicrobial, antioxidant, and antiviral potencies. Various in vitro studies have examined the effect of SeNPs on the virulence of bacteria. This narrative review explores practical issues when using SDF and suggests future directions to develop it, focusing on antimicrobial metals. Several methods are described that could be followed to reduce the discolouration concern, including the use of nanoparticles of silver, of silver fluoride, or of selenium or other metals with antimicrobial actions. ## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9594854/)Abstract

It is generally recognized that the stability of nanoparticles (NPs) has a great impact on their potential biological applications. Despite this, very few studies have investigated the change in toxicity of NPs over time but none has studied the periodic physicochemical changes contributing to it. To address this, we analyzed the effects of long-term storage on the physicochemical changes of green synthesized silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) that directly influences their antimicrobial durability. Light-induced slow synthesis of AgNPs was carried out using _Saraca asoca_ aqueous leaf extract. The synthesis was optimized with respect to parameters known to play a major role in the long-term stability of AgNPs: pH, temperature, light exposure time, AgNO 3 concentration, extract proportion in the reaction mixture and storage conditions. Freshly synthesized AgNPs were characterized and then stored under optimized conditions. UV-vis spectrophotometry, AAS, conventional TEM and HR-TEM along with EDX spectroscopy were used at regular intervals to test the physicochemical properties that influence their long-term stability. Broth dilution assay was used to test antimicrobial activity of AgNPs against _Escherichia coli_ and _Staphylococcus aureus_. Under dark storage conditions at room temperature, the AgNPs exhibited excellent stability with very good dispersity, throughout the study period of 18 months, despite the particles undergoing physicochemical changes in largescale. ## Abstract

keenable.title: Long-Term Physicochemical Stability of Silver and Selenium Nanoparticles Designed for Caries Arrest: A 12-Month Evaluation
keenable.snippet: Purpose: To evaluate the 12-month physicochemical stability of silver and selenium nanoparticles (NPs) fabricated initially for topical caries arrest. Materials and Methods: The nanoparticles were synthesised via chemical reduction and capped with naturally derived agents. Post-synthesis suspensions were washed and stored at 4 °C in the dark for 12 months. Stability was assessed by comparing the physicochemical properties at baseline and 12 months. The characterisation approaches included Tyndall scattering and UV–visible spectroscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy. Results: As formulations aged, they showed differences in stability. Citrate-capped silver NPs (AgL1) retained a defined surface plasmon resonance and showed a 6.7% reduction in elemental concentration. Silver NPs capped with casein (Ag1) and bovine serum albumin (Ag2) showed moderate reductions in elemental concentration (26.9% and 54.8%, respectively), accompanied by the formation of larger particle populations (~20–40 nm). Their initial mean particle sizes were 3.6 ± 3.4 nm for Ag1 and 2.5 ± 0.8 nm for Ag2. In contrast, silver NPs capped with citrate and tannic acid (AgL2) exhibited a substantial reduction in elemental concentration (88.6%), accompanied by pronounced particle aggregation. Selenium nanoparticles were the least stable: UV–Vis absorption features collapsed, TEM showed agglomeration (>70–100 nm), and ICP–OES indicated a significant reduction in the measured elemental concentration in the analysed suspension especially in Se1 (99.9%) and Se2 (99.96%). Conclusions: Under refrigerated, dark storage for 12 months, citrate-capped silver nanoparticles showed preserved integrity, whereas others showed moderate to severe issues with colloidal and elemental stability.

keenable.title: Selenium Nanoparticles: Biomedical Application Advances and New Stomatology Pathways
keenable.snippet: Among various selenium-containing materials, selenium nanoparticles (SeNPs) have attracted extensive interest in agriculture, food science, and medicine18–20 due to their distinctive physicochemical properties and multifunctional advantages. Numerous studies have demonstrated that SeNPs possess higher biocompatibility,21,22 along with remarkable anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and antibacterial activities.23–25 Meanwhile, they are also less toxic and exhibit superior performance in biological systems compared to active selenoproteins or other selenium-containing compounds.26,27 For example, in vitro studies have indicated that chitosan-stabilized SeNPs reduce cytotoxicity by 20–30% relative to sodium selenite and show selective anti-proliferative activity against cancer cells.27 Currently, most reported SeNPs are stabilized with agents such as water-soluble Ganoderma lucidum polysaccharide derivatives,28 SiO~2,~29 or chitosan,30 which enhance their stability and bioactivity. This progress provides an important foundation for their potential applications in stomatology. The core mechanisms of current stabilizers lie in four pathways, including steric effects, potential regulation, chemical bonding and oxidation inhibition.31 For example, chitosan is a commonly used stabilizer for SeNPs. Hector Estevez et al have studied and shown that SeNPs modified by chitosan have a highly positive ζ- potential value of 62.5±5.2 mV that falls in the zone of colloidal stability. Furthermore, experiments have demonstrated that the steric effects of chitosan are also an important mechanism for stabilizing SeNPs. Therefore, chitosan mainly achieves the stability of SeNPs through three pathways: potential regulation, steric hindrance and oxidation inhibition.32

keenable.title: Tailored Synthesis and Profiling of Capped Silver and Selenium Nanoparticles for Topical Applications in Paediatric Dentistry
keenable.snippet:
Silver fluoride (SF) topical solutions effectively arrest caries progression in young children who may not yet comply with standard treatments, which minimises the need for invasive procedures [2]. However, the ionic silver component in these solutions causes permanent tooth staining, raising aesthetic concerns among parents and dental practitioners, limiting their acceptance as a first line treatment option [3].

Among the various nanomaterials explored, silver NPs (AgNPs) are particularly notable for their broad-spectrum antibiofilm efficacy, supporting their integration into dental composites [8], adhesives [9], and implants [10]. Selenium NPs (SeNPs), although less extensively studied in dentistry, are emerging as promising biocompatible antimicrobial agents [11], with additional functions in antioxidant defence and immune modulation [12,13].

In combination, these findings suggest that capped metal NPs could provide improved long-term stability and represent a practical topical antimicrobial choice for caries arrest in paediatric dentistry.

keenable.title: Topically Applied Antimicrobial Silver and Selenium Nanoparticles in Dentistry
keenable.snippet: Dental caries remains a major childhood disease, while anticaries such as silver fluoride use is limited by permanent black staining. This thesis investigated capped silver and selenium nanoparticles as alternative topical anticaries agents in paediatric dentistry. Biocapped nanoparticles were synthesised and characterised using TEM, UV–Vis spectroscopy, ICP–OES, and related techniques. Their antimicrobial activity against Streptococcus mutans and Candida albicans biofilms, staining potential, dentine penetration, and 12-month stability were evaluated in vitro. Silver NPs, particularly citrate-capped formulations, demonstrated strong antimicrobial effects, minimal tooth discolouration, effective dentine infiltration, and superior colloidal stability. These findings support their potential as aesthetically acceptable anticaries nanomaterials.

octen.snippet:
Biofilm-retentive prosthetic and orthodontic appliances create additional caries-prone sites (Preshaw et al., 2011). In orthodontic patients, a meta-analysis of 57 studies involving 9,101 individuals reported white spot lesions in 55% of treated versus 29% of untreated patients, with bonded appliances associated with approximately sevenfold higher odds (Hussain et al., 2025). These settings provide a clinical rationale for materials that actively interfere with cariogenic biofilms rather than functioning only as inert restorative or appliance components.

Accordingly, restorative-material design has progressed from largely inert formulations to antimicrobial and multifunctional bioactive systems that may combine microbial control with remineralization (Melo et al., 2023). Remineralizing agents such as nanohydroxyapatite have shown efficacy in early-lesion models and controlled clinical studies (Amaechi et al., 2019a; Amaechi et al., 2025), but bioactive material design must balance biological activity against esthetic and physicomechanical requirements (Melo et al., 2023).

This narrative review examines seven classes of caries-relevant antimicrobial or antifouling strategies. Six are material-intrinsic: quaternary ammonium compounds (QACs)/quaternary ammonium polyethyleneimine (QPEI) nanoparticles, metallic nanoparticles, photocatalytic titanium-based materials, graphene-based materials, zwitterionic polymers, and biomimetic nanozymes. They are compared by mode of activity (diffusible, contact-dependent, or antifouling) and activation trigger (constitutive, light-activated, or biofilm-microenvironment-responsive).

Antimicrobial peptides constitute the seventh class considered in this review. Unlike the six material-intrinsic classes, their activity is encoded by peptide sequence and molecular design rather than arising from an intrinsic physicochemical property of a dental material.

Abstract

Abstract

Introduction and aims

Silver fluoride is an effective topical agent for arresting early childhood caries. However, its use is somewhat limited by aesthetic concerns, particularly permanent tooth discolouration caused by the precipitation of ionic silver derivatives following application. Nanotechnology offers promising alternative antimicrobial formulations to overcome this limitation. This study evaluated the biofilm inhibition potential of 6 types of silver and selenium nanoparticles, capped with natural materials.

Methods

Using microdilution assays, the minimum biofilm inhibitory concentration and percentage inhibition were measured on single- and dual-species biofilms of Streptococcus mutans and Candida albicans .

Results

Silver nanoparticles, particularly those capped with casein and citrate, demonstrated superior biofilm inhibition, with concentrations of 28.7 and 121.6 µg/mL, achieving 91% and 94% inhibition, respectively. In contrast, selenium nanoparticles required high concentrations to achieve moderate efficacy.

Conclusion

Silver nanoparticles showed significant biofilm inhibitory effects. Further investigations are warranted to evaluate their efficacy against complex multispecies oral biofilms and to determine their long-term stability.

This study evaluated the biofilm inhibition potential of 6 types of silver and selenium nanoparticles, capped with natural materials.
METHODS: Using microdilution assays, the minimum biofilm inhibitory concentration and percentage inhibition were measured on single- and dual-species biofilms of Streptococcus mutans and Candida albicans.
RESULTS: Silver nanoparticles, particularly those capped with casein and citrate, demonstrated superior biofilm inhibition, with concentrations of 28.7 and 121.6 µg/mL, achieving 91% and 94% inhibition, respectively. In contrast, selenium nanoparticles required high concentrations to achieve moderate efficacy.
CONCLUSION: Silver nanoparticles showed significant biofilm inhibitory effects.

# Long-Term Physicochemical Stability of Silver and Selenium Nanoparticles Designed for Caries Arrest: A 12-Month Evaluation
## Abstract
***Purpose*:** To evaluate the 12-month physicochemical stability of silver and selenium nanoparticles (NPs) fabricated initially for topical caries arrest.
***Materials and Methods*:** The nanoparticles were synthesised via chemical reduction and capped with naturally derived agents.
Post-synthesis suspensions were washed and stored at 4 °C in the dark for 12 months.
Stability was assessed by comparing the physicochemical properties at baseline and 12 months.
The characterisation approaches included Tyndall scattering and UV-visible spectroscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy.
***Results*:** As formulations aged, they showed differences in stability.
Citrate-capped silver NPs (AgL1) retained a defined surface plasmon resonance and showed a 6.7% reduction in elemental concentration.
Silver NPs capped with casein (Ag1) and bovine serum albumin (Ag2) showed moderate reductions in elemental concentration (26.9% and 54.8%, respectively), accompanied by the formation of larger particle populations (~20-40 nm).
Their initial mean particle sizes were 3.6 ± 3.4 nm for Ag1 and 2.5 ± 0.8 nm for Ag2.
In contrast, silver NPs capped with citrate and tannic acid (AgL2) exhibited a substantial reduction in elemental concentration (88.6%), accompanied by pronounced particle aggregation.
Selenium nanoparticles were the least stable: UV-Vis absorption features collapsed, TEM showed agglomeration (>70-100 nm), and ICP-OES indicated a significant reduction in the measured elemental concentration in the analysed suspension especially in Se1 (99.9%) and Se2 (99.96%).
***Conclusion* *s*:** Under refrigerated, dark storage for 12 months, citrate-capped silver nanoparticles showed preserved integrity, whereas others showed moderate to severe issues with colloidal and elemental stability.

Early caries lesions, or incipient caries lesions, are characterized by the demineralization of the enamel without cavitation1. These lesions appear as white spots on the enamel surface and indicate subsurface mineral loss. Because early lesions do not exhibit surface breakage in the enamel, they can be reversibly restored by applying appropriate remineralization therapies to restore the mineral content of the enamel and halt the progression of carious lesions2.

ultimate.snippet: Purpose: To evaluate the 12-month physicochemical stability of silver and selenium nanoparticles (NPs) fabricated initially for topical caries arrest. Materials and Methods: The nanoparticles were synthesised via chemical reduction and capped with naturally derived agents. Post-synthesis suspensions were washed and stored at 4 °C in the dark for 12 months. Stability was assessed by comparing the physicochemical properties at baseline and 12 months. The characterisation approaches included Tyndall scattering and UV–visible spectroscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy. Results: As formulations aged, they showed differences in stability. Citrate-capped silver NPs (AgL1) retained a defined surface plasmon resonance and showed a 6.7% reduction in elemental concentration. Silver NPs capped with casein (Ag1) and bovine serum albumin (Ag2) showed moderate reductions in elemental concentration (26.9% and 54.8%, respectively), accompanied by the formation of larger particle populations (~20–40 nm). Their initial mean particle sizes were 3.6 ± 3.4 nm for Ag1 and 2.5 ± 0.8 nm for Ag2. In contrast, silver NPs capped with citrate and tannic acid (AgL2) exhibited a substantial reduction in elemental concentration (88.6%), accompanied by pronounced particle aggregation. Selenium nanoparticles were the least stable: UV–Vis absorption features collapsed, TEM showed agglomeration (>70–100 nm), and ICP–OES indicated a significant reduction in the measured elemental concentration in the analysed suspension especially in Se1 (99.9%) and Se2 (99.96%). Conclusions: Under refrigerated, dark storage for 12 months, citrate-capped silver nanoparticles showed preserved integrity, whereas others showed moderate to severe issues with colloidal and elemental stability.

ultimate.snippet: Among various selenium-containing materials, selenium nanoparticles (SeNPs) have attracted extensive interest in agriculture, food science, and medicine18–20 due to their distinctive physicochemical properties and multifunctional advantages. Numerous studies have demonstrated that SeNPs possess higher biocompatibility,21,22 along with remarkable anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and antibacterial activities.23–25 Meanwhile, they are also less toxic and exhibit superior performance in biological systems compared to active selenoproteins or other selenium-containing compounds.26,27 For example, in vitro studies have indicated that chitosan-stabilized SeNPs reduce cytotoxicity by 20–30% relative to sodium selenite and show selective anti-proliferative activity against cancer cells.27 Currently, most reported SeNPs are stabilized with agents such as water-soluble Ganoderma lucidum polysaccharide derivatives,28 SiO~2,~29 or chitosan,30 which enhance their stability and bioactivity. This progress provides an important foundation for their potential applications in stomatology. The core mechanisms of current stabilizers lie in four pathways, including steric effects, potential regulation, chemical bonding and oxidation inhibition.31 For example, chitosan is a commonly used stabilizer for SeNPs. Hector Estevez et al have studied and shown that SeNPs modified by chitosan have a highly positive ζ- potential value of 62.5±5.2 mV that falls in the zone of colloidal stability. Furthermore, experiments have demonstrated that the steric effects of chitosan are also an important mechanism for stabilizing SeNPs. Therefore, chitosan mainly achieves the stability of SeNPs through three pathways: potential regulation, steric hindrance and oxidation inhibition.32

Materials and methods: Gels without antimicrobial agents (G0), with 0.12% β-AgVO 3 (G1), and with 0.12% chlorhexidine (G2) were prepared and stored for 12 months. Physicochemical properties (organoleptic characteristics, pH, and spreadability) and antimicrobial activity against Candida albicans and Streptococcus mutans were evaluated.

Results: G1 exhibited progressive physicochemical instability, including color change, reduced pH, and increased spreadability, whereas G0 remained stable. Structural changes in the nanomaterial were observed after storage.
